LLM Inference Systems

Why serving is a memory-bandwidth problem wearing a compute costume — and what that implies for silicon.

§How to use this document

Fourth in a series with the Recurrent Depth, Sparse Attention and Linear Attention guides. Those three are about changing the model to make serving cheaper. This one is about serving the model you have — and it is written for someone who will eventually have to decide what to put on a die.

  • Pass 1. §0–§1. The roofline and the arithmetic. If you can derive the saturation batch size and the KV cache size from memory, every optimisation in §2–§7 becomes obvious rather than arbitrary.
  • Pass 2. §2–§7. The six families of optimisation, roughly in the order a serving stack applies them.
  • Pass 3. §8–§9. The hardware landscape, what the workload actually asks of silicon, and a worked capacity plan.

Assumed background: transformer inference at the level of "there is a prefill and there is a decode," and comfort with back-of-envelope arithmetic. Everything else is derived.

If a term is unfamiliar, it is defined. Appendix B builds the roofline model from scratch and explains the GPU, interconnect, systems and numerics vocabulary (SM, GEMM/GEMV, all-to-all, RDMA, copy-on-write, radix tree, E4M3/E2M1/E8M0, block scaling, rejection sampling). Appendix C is a one-line glossary.

The thesis, up front

Autoregressive decode reads the entire model — and the entire KV cache — from HBM to produce one token per sequence. Its weight-only batch-one intensity is ~1 FLOP/byte at BF16 or ~2 at FP8, against a precision-dependent hardware balance point often in the hundreds. Almost every technique in this document is a way of raising that ratio: batch more sequences over one weight read, shrink the bytes, or find more arithmetic to do per byte. Once you see decode as a bandwidth problem, the whole field organises itself.

0The mental model

0.1 Two phases with opposite characters

PrefillDecode
What happensProcess the whole prompt in one forward passGenerate one token per sequence, per step, autoregressively
Matrix shapesn×dn\times dn×d times d×dd\times dd×d — big GEMMsB×dB\times dB×d times d×dd\times dd×d — skinny GEMMs / GEMV-like
Bound byComputeMemory bandwidth
Saturates atBatch size 1–2 (one long prompt already fills the machine)Hundreds of concurrent sequences
Latency metricTTFT — time to first tokenTPOT / ITL — time per output token
Scales withPrompt length (quadratically in attention)Number of generated tokens, linearly; and with context length through the KV read
Why this one plot drives everything

The two phases want opposite things from the scheduler, from the parallelism strategy, and arguably from the hardware. Prefill wants to run alone and finish fast; decode wants to wait for company. Colocating them on the same GPU means every long prefill stalls every decode in flight — which is the tension §3 and §5 exist to resolve.

0.2 The roofline, and the one number to memorise

I=FLOPs performedbytes moved,I∗=FpeakβpeakIH100,BF16∗=989 TFLOP/s3.35 TB/s≈295 FLOP/byteIH200,BF16∗=9894.80≈206 FLOP/byteIB200,BF16∗=22508.00≈281 FLOP/byteIB200,FP4∗=90008.00=1125 FLOP/byte(dense)I<I∗: memory-bound,I>I∗: compute-bound\begin{aligned}I&=\frac{\text{FLOPs performed}}{\text{bytes moved}},\quad I^*=\frac{F_{\mathrm{peak}}}{\beta_{\mathrm{peak}}}\\I^*_{\mathrm{H100,BF16}}&=\frac{989\,\mathrm{TFLOP/s}}{3.35\,\mathrm{TB/s}}\approx295\,\mathrm{FLOP/byte}\\I^*_{\mathrm{H200,BF16}}&=\frac{989}{4.80}\approx206\,\mathrm{FLOP/byte}\\I^*_{\mathrm{B200,BF16}}&=\frac{2250}{8.00}\approx281\,\mathrm{FLOP/byte}\\I^*_{\mathrm{B200,FP4}}&=\frac{9000}{8.00}=1125\,\mathrm{FLOP/byte}\quad\text{(dense)}\\I<I^*&:\ \text{memory-bound},\qquad I>I^*:\ \text{compute-bound}\end{aligned}IIH100,BF16∗​IH200,BF16∗​IB200,BF16∗​IB200,FP4∗​I<I∗​=bytes movedFLOPs performed​,I∗=βpeak​Fpeak​​=3.35TB/s989TFLOP/s​≈295FLOP/byte=4.80989​≈206FLOP/byte=8.002250​≈281FLOP/byte=8.009000​=1125FLOP/byte(dense): memory-bound,I>I∗: compute-bound​

Now compute the intensity of batch-1 decode. Per token, a dense model performs about 2N2N2N FLOPs (NNN = parameter count, one multiply-add each) and must read N⋅pN\cdot pN⋅p bytes of weights:

Idecode,B=1=2NNp=2p=1 FLOP/byte(BF16)\begin{aligned}I_{\mathrm{decode},B=1}&=\frac{2N}{Np}=\frac2p=1\,\mathrm{FLOP/byte}\quad\text{(BF16)}\end{aligned}Idecode,B=1​​=Np2N​=p2​=1FLOP/byte(BF16)​

One, against a ridge point of roughly three hundred. Batch-1 decode uses about 0.3% of a GPU's arithmetic capability. This is not an implementation failure — it is the workload. The entire discipline of inference optimisation is the search for ways to get that number up.

Note what FP4 does to the picture

Lower precision can reduce weight traffic and increase native arithmetic throughput. Under a weight-only roofline, if peak compute doubles while bytes per weight halve, the saturation batch stays approximately unchanged because it depends on their product. The dense B200 FP4 ridge is about 1,125 FLOP/byte using 9 PFLOP/s and 8 TB/s. Real latency gains depend on scale metadata, kernel support, dequantization, KV traffic, and the precision used by each operator; halving payload bytes does not guarantee a 2× request speedup.

Derivation: derive the ridge point without mixing dense and sparse peaks

Definitions. A kernel performs f FLOPs and moves m bytes across the memory boundary being analyzed. Let F be the relevant compute ceiling in FLOP/s and Bw the bandwidth in byte/s. Even with perfect overlap, it cannot finish faster than either required resource time:

t≥max⁡(fF,mBw)Fachieved≤fmax⁡(f/F,m/Bw)=min⁡(F,Bwfm)I=fm,I∗=FBw\begin{aligned}t&\ge\max\left(\frac fF,\frac m{B_w}\right)\\F_{\mathrm{achieved}}&\le\frac f{\max(f/F,m/B_w)}=\min\left(F,B_w\frac fm\right)\\I&=\frac fm,\quad I^*=\frac F{B_w}\end{aligned}tFachieved​I​≥max(Ff​,Bw​m​)≤max(f/F,m/Bw​)f​=min(F,Bw​mf​)=mf​,I∗=Bw​F​​

Use the peak for the arithmetic actually executed. A structured-sparse tensor-core figure assumes supported sparsity and counts its effective operations; it is not the dense peak for a dense checkpoint. NVIDIA lists H100/H200 SXM FP8 at 3,958 TFLOP/s with sparsity, corresponding to about 1,979 TFLOP/s dense. For eight B200s, the current HGX table gives 72 PFLOP/s sparse FP8, hence 36 PFLOP/s dense per system or 4.5 PFLOP/s per GPU. Its FP4 system figures are explicitly 144 sparse / 72 dense, or 9 PFLOP/s dense per GPU. H100 specification and footnote; H200 specification and footnote; HGX specifications.

The B200 dense FP4 ridge with 8 TB/s is therefore 9·10¹⁵/(8·10¹²)=1,125 FLOP/byte. For weights of N parameters and b bytes each, a B-sequence decode GEMM does roughly 2NB FLOPs while reading Nb weight bytes, so its weight-only intensity is 2B/b. Equating this with F/Bw gives Bsat=Fb/(2Bw). If lowering precision doubles F and halves b, the product Fb is unchanged: quantization does not automatically raise the saturation batch. Real changes depend on effective metadata bytes, kernel efficiency, activation precision, and dequantization.

Exercise — Spot the sparse-peak factor-of-two error

A GPU lists FP8 4 PFLOP/s with structured sparsity, dense FP8 at half that rate, and HBM bandwidth 4 TB/s. Weights use one byte each. Compute the dense FP8 ridge and weight-only saturation batch. What would using the sparse peak incorrectly predict?

Show worked solution

Dense F=2·10¹⁵ FLOP/s, so I*=2·10¹⁵/(4·10¹²)=500 FLOP/byte. Weight-only intensity is 2B, giving Bsat=250. Substituting 4 PFLOP/s without a sparse workload gives I*=1000 and Bsat=500, both twice the appropriate dense values. The mathematical roofline is correct in both calculations; the second calculation uses an inapplicable hardware ceiling.

0.3 The metrics, and why "throughput" is not one of them

MetricDefinitionWho cares
TTFTTime to first token — queueing + prefillInteractive users. Dominated by prompt length and by queueing behind other prefills.
TPOT / ITLTime per output token, after the firstPerceived streaming speed. Must beat reading speed (~20–30 tok/s) to feel fluid.
ThroughputTotal tokens/s across all requestsYour finance team. Maximised by huge batches, which destroys TPOT.
GoodputRequests/s served within the SLOThe only metric that is actually well-posed. A system at 10× throughput that misses every latency target has goodput zero.

Throughput and latency trade off directly through batch size, so a throughput number without a latency constraint is meaningless. Always state the SLO. The literature's term of art for "throughput subject to SLO" is goodput, and it is the right optimisation target.

1The arithmetic

Five formulas. If you can reproduce these on a whiteboard you can size any deployment and evaluate any optimisation claim.

1.1 FLOPs and bytes per token

N=parameters,p=bytes/parameter,B=batch sizen=context length,L=layers,HKV=KV heads,dh=head widthFstep≈2NB⏟dense+4BndL⏟attentionMstep≈Np⏟weights read once/batch+2BnHKVdhLp⏟KV read per sequence\begin{aligned}N&=\text{parameters},\quad p=\text{bytes/parameter},\quad B=\text{batch size}\\n&=\text{context length},\quad L=\text{layers},\quad H_{\mathrm{KV}}=\text{KV heads},\quad d_h=\text{head width}\\F_{\mathrm{step}}&\approx\underbrace{2NB}_{\mathrm{dense}}+\underbrace{4BndL}_{\mathrm{attention}}\\M_{\mathrm{step}}&\approx\underbrace{Np}_{\text{weights read once/batch}}+\underbrace{2BnH_{\mathrm{KV}}d_hLp}_{\text{KV read per sequence}}\end{aligned}NnFstep​Mstep​​=parameters,p=bytes/parameter,B=batch size=context length,L=layers,HKV​=KV heads,dh​=head width≈dense2NB​​+attention4BndL​​≈weights read once/batchNp​​+KV read per sequence2BnHKV​dh​Lp​​​
The asymmetry that explains everything

Weight bytes are approximately independent of batch size when loaded once per step; KV bytes are proportional to it for independent sequences. Increasing BBB amortises weight traffic, giving near-linear throughput gains initially and diminishing returns as KV traffic or compute becomes important. Every serving system lives at the knee of that curve, and every memory optimisation in §2 exists to push the knee further right.

1.2 The saturation batch size BsatB_{\mathrm{sat}}Bsat​

At what batch size does decode stop being memory-bound? Ignore KV for a moment and equate the two times:

tmemory=NpBW,tcompute=2NBFBsat=Fp2BWBH100,BF16=989⋅1012⋅22⋅3.35⋅1012≈295BH100,FP8=1.979⋅10152⋅3.35⋅1012≈295(dense peak)BB200,BF16=2.25⋅1015⋅22⋅8⋅1012≈281BB200,FP4=9⋅1015⋅0.52⋅8⋅1012≈281(payload bytes only)\begin{aligned}t_{\mathrm{memory}}&=\frac{Np}{\mathrm{BW}},\quad t_{\mathrm{compute}}=\frac{2NB}F\\B_{\mathrm{sat}}&=\frac{Fp}{2\mathrm{BW}}\\B_{\mathrm{H100,BF16}}&=\frac{989\cdot10^{12}\cdot2}{2\cdot3.35\cdot10^{12}}\approx295\\B_{\mathrm{H100,FP8}}&=\frac{1.979\cdot10^{15}}{2\cdot3.35\cdot10^{12}}\approx295\quad\text{(dense peak)}\\B_{\mathrm{B200,BF16}}&=\frac{2.25\cdot10^{15}\cdot2}{2\cdot8\cdot10^{12}}\approx281\\B_{\mathrm{B200,FP4}}&=\frac{9\cdot10^{15}\cdot0.5}{2\cdot8\cdot10^{12}}\approx281\quad\text{(payload bytes only)}\end{aligned}tmemory​Bsat​BH100,BF16​BH100,FP8​BB200,BF16​BB200,FP4​​=BWNp​,tcompute​=F2NB​=2BWFp​=2⋅3.35⋅1012989⋅1012⋅2​≈295=2⋅3.35⋅10121.979⋅1015​≈295(dense peak)=2⋅8⋅10122.25⋅1015⋅2​≈281=2⋅8⋅10129⋅1015⋅0.5​≈281(payload bytes only)​

Three consequences worth stating explicitly:

  • When weight traffic dominates and the kernel sustains similar bandwidth, step time can be approximately flat over a batch range. KV reads and attention FLOPs grow with batch, so this is a regime-specific approximation rather than a guarantee that 1 and 200 sequences cost the same.
  • BsatB_{\mathrm{sat}}Bsat​ is in the hundreds. Hitting it requires hundreds of concurrent sequences resident in HBM, which requires their KV caches to fit — which is why memory management (§2) is the gating technology for throughput.
  • Quantization changes BsatB_{\mathrm{sat}}Bsat​ through the product F·p. A proportional compute increase and byte reduction cancel in the weight-only formula. Different kernels, effective metadata bytes, or weight-only arithmetic can change the result; use the actual execution format.

Derivation: derive the saturation batch when KV traffic also grows with batch

One decode step, homogeneous context lengths. Let W be weight bytes read once for the batch, k be KV and other per-sequence bytes read each step, and f be per-sequence FLOPs including attention. Approximate total traffic by W+Bk and FLOPs by Bf. This assumes one weight read, no cross-sequence KV reuse, and an effective bandwidth/compute rate that is locally constant.

  1. The intensity is I(B)=Bf/(W+Bk).
  2. Set compute time Bf/F equal to memory time (W+Bk)/Bw.
  3. Collect B terms: B(fBw−Fk)=FW.
Bsat=FWfBw−Fkonly if fBw−Fk>0lim⁡B→∞I(B)=fkfk≤FBw⟹no finite compute-bound crossoverRmemory=BBwW+Bk⟶Bwk\begin{aligned}B_{\mathrm{sat}}&=\frac{FW}{fB_w-Fk}\quad\text{only if }fB_w-Fk>0\\\lim_{B\to\infty}I(B)&=\frac fk\\\frac fk\le\frac F{B_w}&\Longrightarrow\text{no finite compute-bound crossover}\\R_{\mathrm{memory}}&=\frac{BB_w}{W+Bk}\longrightarrow\frac{B_w}k\end{aligned}Bsat​B→∞lim​I(B)kf​≤Bw​F​Rmemory​​=fBw​−FkFW​only if fBw​−Fk>0=kf​⟹no finite compute-bound crossover=W+BkBBw​​⟶kBw​​​

The derivative of the memory-bound throughput is BwW/(W+Bk)²>0, and its second derivative is negative. Batching gives diminishing returns, not superlinear returns. At long context, k grows and the asymptote can stay far below the compute ridge. This is why the statement “large batch means compute bound” is conditional, and why KV-aware speculative decoding can help in some large-batch regimes.

Numerical illustration: W=100 GB, f=200 GFLOPs per sequence, F=1 PFLOP/s, and Bw=5 TB/s. With k=0.5 GB, f/k=400 FLOP/byte exceeds the ridge 200, and Bsat=200. With k=2 GB, f/k=100 falls below the ridge; no batch makes the model compute limited under these assumptions. Real kernels can change utilization before this ideal crossover, so measure the curve.

Exercise — Prove that more batching cannot cross the ridge

Take W=60 GB, k=1 GB per sequence, f=150 GFLOPs, F=1.2 PFLOP/s, and Bw=4 TB/s. Does a finite saturation batch exist? Give the asymptotic bandwidth-limited tokens/s and explain its units.

Show worked solution

The ridge is 1.2·10¹⁵/(4·10¹²)=300 FLOP/byte, while f/k=150 FLOP/byte. The intensity approaches 150 from below, so no finite batch crosses 300. The traffic-bound throughput approaches Bw/k=4·10¹²/10⁹=4,000 sequence tokens/s. This is aggregate output tokens per second, with one token per active sequence per step; it is not 4,000 tokens/s for each user.

1.3 The KV cache, sized properly

cKV=2LHKVdhpLlama-3-70B GQA: c=2⋅80⋅8⋅128⋅2=327,680 B=320 KiBM(131,072)=42.95 GB=40 GiBper sequence on an 80 GB H100MHA (H=64):c=2⋅80⋅64⋅128⋅2≈2.6 MB(8×)M(131,072)=343.60 GB=320 GiBDeepSeek-V3 MLA: c=(512+64)⋅61⋅2≈70 kB/tokenAbout 4.5× smaller than this GQA cache.\begin{aligned}c_{\mathrm{KV}}&=2LH_{\mathrm{KV}}d_hp\\\text{Llama-3-70B GQA: }c&=2\cdot80\cdot8\cdot128\cdot2=327{,}680\,\mathrm B=320\,\mathrm{KiB}\\M(131{,}072)&=42.95\,\mathrm{GB}=40\,\mathrm{GiB}\quad\text{per sequence on an 80 GB H100}\\\text{MHA }(H=64):\quad c&=2\cdot80\cdot64\cdot128\cdot2\approx2.6\,\mathrm{MB}\quad(8\times)\\M(131{,}072)&=343.60\,\mathrm{GB}=320\,\mathrm{GiB}\\\text{DeepSeek-V3 MLA: }c&=(512+64)\cdot61\cdot2\approx70\,\mathrm{kB/token}\\&\text{About }4.5\times\text{ smaller than this GQA cache.}\end{aligned}cKV​Llama-3-70B GQA: cM(131,072)MHA (H=64):cM(131,072)DeepSeek-V3 MLA: c​=2LHKV​dh​p=2⋅80⋅8⋅128⋅2=327,680B=320KiB=42.95GB=40GiBper sequence on an 80 GB H100=2⋅80⋅64⋅128⋅2≈2.6MB(8×)=343.60GB=320GiB=(512+64)⋅61⋅2≈70kB/tokenAbout 4.5× smaller than this GQA cache.​

At 128K context on an H100 with 70B BF16 weights (140 GB, so already multi-GPU), a single 131,072-token sequence's BF16 KV cache is about 42.95 GB (40 GiB). That is the whole story of why long context is expensive and why MQA/GQA/MLA were adopted so fast: they are not accuracy improvements, they are the difference between 4 concurrent sequences and 40.

Capacity is not latency

Longer context raises KV storage and per-sequence traffic. At a fixed batch it can slow each user; at a fixed memory budget it also reduces the number of users served concurrently. The similar step floors across the full-memory examples arise because their different batch sizes consume similar total KV capacity. They do not imply that one user’s latency is independent of context.

Derivation: derive exact KV capacity and distinguish it from latency

Layer-dependent cache. For layer ℓ, let Hkv,ℓ be KV heads, dk,ℓ and dv,ℓ the stored widths, and bk,ℓ, bv,ℓ their bytes per scalar. The bytes added by one token are c=∑ℓHkv,ℓ(dk,ℓbk,ℓ+dv,ℓbv,ℓ)c=\sum_\ell H_{\mathrm{kv},\ell}(d_{k,\ell}b_{k,\ell}+d_{v,\ell}b_{v,\ell})c=∑ℓ​Hkv,ℓ​(dk,ℓ​bk,ℓ​+dv,ℓ​bv,ℓ​), plus scales and metadata. A compressed MLA latent uses its actual stored dimensions instead of adding reconstructed K/V dimensions.

c=2LHKVdb(uniform ordinary KV)Mseq=ncC=Mdevice−Mweights−Mruntime−MreserveBmem=⌊Cnc⌋(equal sequence lengths)\begin{aligned}c&=2LH_{\mathrm{KV}}db\quad\text{(uniform ordinary KV)}\\M_{\mathrm{seq}}&=nc\\C&=M_{\mathrm{device}}-M_{\mathrm{weights}}-M_{\mathrm{runtime}}-M_{\mathrm{reserve}}\\B_{\mathrm{mem}}&=\left\lfloor\frac C{nc}\right\rfloor\quad\text{(equal sequence lengths)}\end{aligned}cMseq​CBmem​​=2LHKV​db(uniform ordinary KV)=nc=Mdevice​−Mweights​−Mruntime​−Mreserve​=⌊ncC​⌋(equal sequence lengths)​

For the H200 teaching example, c=163,840 bytes with FP8 GQA, and C=61·10⁹ bytes. At n=8,192, one sequence uses 1,342,177,280 bytes, so Bmem=45; at 32,768 it is 11; at 131,072 it is 2. Fractional results cannot be rounded up. Output growth and cache metadata need additional reserve, so these are instantaneous upper bounds under the idealized ledger.

Latency is a separate calculation. A full-KV decode reads approximately W+Bnc bytes per step. At B=1, increasing context from 8,192 to 131,072 changes the H200 bandwidth-only floor from (70+1.342)/4.8≈14.863 ms to (70+21.475)/4.8≈19.057 ms, with GB/TB units converted consistently. Long context can therefore slow an individual request and reduce the number of concurrent requests. Filling all available memory makes Bnc roughly constant, which can disguise this effect when comparing different batch sizes.

Exercise — Do not spend the same quantization saving twice

A cache budget is 48 GiB, and a sequence needs 1.5 GiB when KV is already FP8. How many equal sequences fit? A plan then says “enable FP8 to double this number.” Identify the error and give the BF16 baseline under the same idealized assumptions.

Show worked solution

At FP8, floor(48/1.5)=32 sequences fit. The plan has already counted FP8, so enabling it again produces no further saving. If BF16 uses exactly twice the cache bytes and metadata is ignored, each sequence uses 3 GiB and the baseline capacity is 16. The genuine FP8 improvement is 16→32, not 32→64. Capacity does not by itself certify that either batch satisfies a latency target.

2Memory management: making the batch fit

If throughput is set by concurrency and concurrency is set by KV capacity, then memory allocation is the throughput optimisation.

2.1 The waste problem

2.2 PagedAttention — virtual memory for the KV cache

Two consequences beyond the obvious memory saving, both of which matter more than the saving itself:

  • Copy-on-write sharing. Parallel sampling, beam search and — most importantly — shared system prompts can point at the same physical blocks. A production workload with a 2000-token shared system prompt across thousands of requests stores it once.
  • Prefix caching. Extend sharing across requests and over time and you get automatic prefix reuse; SGLang's RadixAttention organises the blocks in a radix tree so any common prefix is found and reused. For agent workloads that re-send a growing conversation every turn, this is frequently the single largest win available — it converts repeated prefill into a cache hit.

2.3 Shrinking the cache at the source

TechniqueMechanismTypical saving / cost
MQA / GQAShare K,V across query heads (one group per GGG heads)8× at GGG=8. Near-free in quality when trained in; now universal.
MLACompress K,V into a low-rank latent, decompress inside the kernelAnother ~4× over GQA. Trades bandwidth for arithmetic — a good trade in a memory-bound regime.
KV quantizationStore the cache at FP8 or INT4 with per-block scales2–4×. Keys are more sensitive than values; per-channel scaling for keys, per-token for values is the usual recipe.
Cross-layer sharingReuse one layer's KV for several layersProportional to sharing factor; quality cost is real and model-dependent.
Sliding window layersBound the cache per layer at www tokensEnormous at long context. Interleave with a few global layers — see the sparse and linear attention guides.
Eviction / selectionDrop or skip KV entries (H2O, Quest, DSA)See the sparse attention guide. Composes awkwardly with paging.
Offload to CPU / SSDPage cold blocks out over PCIe or NVMePrefix reuse is often the most favorable case. Live-KV offload is possible with selective reads, overlap, CPU-side computation, or relaxed latency targets, but transferring a full large cache every token across PCIe can dominate decode time; compare required bytes with effective tier bandwidth.

Derivation: derive paged allocation waste and prefix-sharing savings

Fixed token blocks. Let a physical KV block hold P tokens, each costing c bytes across the layers being allocated. A request of length n needs ceil(n/P) blocks. Its unused token slots are w(n)=Pceil(n/P)−n, so 0≤w≤P−1. For B independent requests, internal waste is less than BPc bytes; no maximum-output-length reservation is required just to address the cache.

If the nonzero final-block occupancy is uniform over 1,…,P, expected waste is (P−1)/2 slots per request. Uniform occupancy is a workload assumption, not a theorem about real prompts. Block tables, refcounts, allocator metadata, and unused reserved pools add separate overhead. Paging bounds one kind of fragmentation; it does not turn all device memory into usable KV.

Mno share=B(s+u)cMshare=sc+BucΔM=(B−1)scCommon prefix s, private suffix u; exact reuse, partial blocks omitted.\begin{aligned}M_{\mathrm{no\ share}}&=B(s+u)c\\M_{\mathrm{share}}&=sc+Buc\\\Delta M&=(B-1)sc\\&\text{Common prefix }s\text{, private suffix }u\text{; exact reuse, partial blocks omitted.}\end{aligned}Mno share​Mshare​ΔM​=B(s+u)c=sc+Buc=(B−1)scCommon prefix s, private suffix u; exact reuse, partial blocks omitted.​

Share a block only when the cached state is valid for the same model, adapter, token history, positions, masks, and relevant runtime configuration. Matching text fragments at different histories are not necessarily matching KV. Full prefix blocks can remain shared; appending to a partially filled shared block may require copy-on-write. Prefix sharing saves capacity and prefill work. During decode, independent requests may still read the shared prefix, so the traffic saving depends on whether the kernel/cache hierarchy actually reuses those reads across requests.

Exercise — Compute fragmentation and shared-prefix capacity

Let P=16, c=256 KiB per token, and four request lengths be 17,31,32,33. How many blocks and wasted slots are allocated? Separately, 100 requests share a 1,024-token prefix and each has a 256-token private suffix; ignore metadata and all partial blocks. Find the shared/unshared capacity ratio.

Show worked solution

The block counts are 2,2,2,3, totaling 9 blocks or 144 slots. Actual tokens total 113, so 31 slots are wasted, occupying 31·256 KiB=7.75 MiB. For prefix sharing, unshared tokens are 100·1280=128,000; shared tokens are 1024+100·256=26,624. The ratio is 26,624/128,000=0.208, a capacity reduction of 79.2% under these assumptions. This does not imply the same percentage reduction in decode traffic.

3Scheduling: the batch is the product

Given fixed hardware and a fixed model, the scheduler decides your cost per token.

3.1 From static to continuous batching

Continuous batching (introduced by Orca, now universal) is the largest single throughput win in the stack — often several times — for a simple reason: without it, GPU slots sit idle waiting for the longest sequence in a batch, and output lengths vary by an order of magnitude.

3.2 The prefill–decode interference problem

Continuous batching creates a new problem. When a new request arrives, its prefill must run. A 4000-token prefill takes maybe 200 ms; during that step, every sequence already decoding gets nothing. Their TPOT spikes. You now face a direct choice:

  • Prefill-prioritising → good TTFT, terrible tail TPOT (generation stalls).
  • Decode-prioritising → smooth TPOT, terrible TTFT under load (head-of-line blocking).
Chunked prefill — the standard answer

Split a long prefill into chunks of a few hundred tokens and co-schedule one chunk alongside the decode batch in each iteration. The decode tokens ride along in the same kernels — and since decode is memory-bound and prefill is compute-bound, they use different resources, so the combined step is barely slower than the prefill chunk alone. This is "stall-free batching," and Sarathi-Serve reports 2.6–5.6× better throughput–latency trade-offs than vLLM. If you tune one thing in a serving stack after enabling continuous batching, tune the chunk size.

Other scheduler concerns that bite in production: admission control (refuse rather than accept and miss the SLO), preemption (swap a sequence's KV to CPU or recompute it when memory runs out — recomputation is often cheaper than swapping, because PCIe is slow), fairness (one 200K-token request can monopolise the cache), and length prediction (knowing output length in advance would make scheduling tractable; nobody does it reliably).

Derivation: derive useful batch occupancy and a chunk-size latency budget

Static batch toy model. B requests have output lengths m₁,…,mB, and a static padded batch runs max mi steps at approximately constant step cost. Useful token slots are Σmi, but allocated slots are Bmax mi. Thus useful occupancy is U=Σmi/(Bmax mi). Continuous batching replaces finished requests and can raise U, provided queued work, memory, and latency constraints permit refill. It cannot exceed full utilization, and a variable-cost kernel needs a time-weighted version.

Chunked prefill. Let a decode batch already take td. Suppose profiling locally fits a co-scheduled prefill chunk of C tokens with incremental time aC+tlaunch, where a depends on context, batch, and the kernel. To maintain a per-iteration latency budget τ:

td+aC+tlaunch≤τC≤τ−td−tlauncha\begin{aligned}t_d+aC+t_{\mathrm{launch}}&\le\tau\\C&\le\frac{\tau-t_d-t_{\mathrm{launch}}}a\end{aligned}td​+aC+tlaunch​C​≤τ≤aτ−td​−tlaunch​​​

If τ=25 ms, td=10 ms, tlaunch=1 ms and a=0.02 ms/token, the bound gives C≤700. This is a fitted local scheduling rule, not a universal 700-token recommendation. Quadratic attention, changing batch size, and shared-resource contention can make the fit invalid. Prefill and decode do not literally use disjoint hardware; co-scheduling benefits from improved reuse and utilization, while still consuming common tensor cores and memory bandwidth.

Queue consistency. In a stable system, Little’s law is mean active requests B̄=λE[D], where λ is admitted requests/s and D is mean time in the measured subsystem. Aggregate output throughput is λE[m]. “1,000 concurrent users” is not an arrival rate until response lengths, think time, and latency are specified. A utilization target close to one also increases queueing risk; a kernel roofline does not include waiting time or tail SLO violations.

Exercise — Relate occupancy, arrivals, and active requests

A padded batch has output lengths (20,20,20,100). Compute useful slot occupancy. A separate stable service admits 5 requests/s, each spends 8 s actively generating and emits 200 tokens on average. Find mean active requests and output throughput. Is 40 active requests an input arrival rate?

Show worked solution

Useful occupancy is (20+20+20+100)/(4·100)=160/400=0.4. Under the ideal constant-step model, 60% of allocated slots are wasted. For the service, Little’s law gives B̄=5·8=40 active requests. Output throughput is 5·200=1,000 tokens/s. Forty is concurrency, measured in requests, whereas arrival rate is 5 requests/s; confusing them loses the time dimension.

4Kernels and parallelism

4.1 Kernels

  • FlashAttention (1/2/3) — tiled, fused, exact attention that never materialises the n×nn\times nn×n matrix. The prefill workhorse. See the sparse attention guide for the mechanism.
  • FlashDecoding — at batch 1 and long context, attention decode has only B×HB \times HB×H units of parallelism, which does not fill a GPU with 132 SMs. Split the KV dimension across SMs and combine partial softmax results. A pure occupancy fix, and a large one.
  • Paged attention kernels — gather KV by block table. Note this is a genuine cost: the gather breaks the perfectly coalesced access a contiguous cache would allow, which is why block size is a tuned parameter (too small: pointer-chasing; too large: fragmentation).
  • Fusion and CUDA graphs — at batch 1, kernel launch overhead is a measurable fraction of step time. Capturing the whole decode step as a graph removes per-kernel launch cost. Unglamorous and worth 10–20%.
  • Fused MoE kernels — grouped GEMM so that experts with different token counts run in one launch.

4.2 Parallelism, and what it costs

StrategySplitsCommunication
Tensor (TP)Each layer's matrices across GPUsTwo all-reduces per layer, on the critical path. Only sane within a node over NVLink. Reduces latency; scales sub-linearly.
Pipeline (PP)Layers across GPUsPoint-to-point activations only — cheap, works across nodes. Adds bubbles; helps throughput, not latency.
Expert (EP)MoE experts across GPUsAll-to-all, twice per MoE layer. The hardest communication pattern in the stack.
Data (DP)Whole replicasNone. Always the first choice if the model fits.

The rule of thumb: TP within a node, PP or DP across nodes. TP's all-reduces are latency-critical and NVLink (900 GB/s on Hopper, 1.8 TB/s on Blackwell) is 10–20× faster than InfiniBand; crossing a node boundary with TP is usually a mistake.

MoE inference is a different animal

An MoE model reads the weights of every activated expert but each expert only processes the tokens routed to it. If 8 of 256 experts fire per token, a batch of BBB tokens spreads over many experts and each sees a small slice — so the effective batch per expert, which is what determines arithmetic intensity, is far below BBB. MoE therefore needs a much larger global batch than a dense model to leave the memory-bound regime, plus all-to-all communication to get tokens to their experts. The standard answer is large-scale expert parallelism with heavily optimised all-to-all kernels (DeepEP and similar) and aggressive computation/communication overlap. If you are designing hardware and your target workload is MoE, the interconnect is at least as important as the compute.

Derivation: derive the tensor-parallel communication floor

A ring model, not a topology-independent law. Let P GPUs all-reduce an activation tensor of m bytes per GPU. An ideal ring performs P−1 reduce-scatter steps and P−1 all-gather steps; each step sends m/P bytes. With startup latency α per step and effective link bandwidth Blink:

tallreduce≈2(P−1)α+2(P−1)mPBlinkTcollective≈2LtallreduceTwo sequential all-reduces/layer, before overlap or algorithm changes.\begin{aligned}t_{\mathrm{allreduce}}&\approx2(P-1)\alpha+\frac{2(P-1)m}{PB_{\mathrm{link}}}\\T_{\mathrm{collective}}&\approx2L t_{\mathrm{allreduce}}\\&\text{Two sequential all-reduces/layer, before overlap or algorithm changes.}\end{aligned}tallreduce​Tcollective​​≈2(P−1)α+PBlink​2(P−1)m​≈2Ltallreduce​Two sequential all-reduces/layer, before overlap or algorithm changes.​

The first term dominates tiny decode tensors, while the bandwidth term matters for larger prefill tensors. Increasing P reduces each GPU’s weight/compute share, but it does not eliminate startup latency. A basic no-overlap comparison is TTP≈Tlocal(P)+TcollectiveT_{\mathrm{TP}}\approx T_{\mathrm{local}}(P)+T_{\mathrm{collective}}TTP​≈Tlocal​(P)+Tcollective​; TP helps latency only if the reduced local time exceeds the added communication. Tree, hierarchical, reduce-scatter-based, or fused implementations have different constants and dependency structures. Advertised bidirectional aggregate NVLink bandwidth is not automatically the unidirectional effective Blink for this formula.

Pipeline parallelism has a different trade. For P equal-cost stages and M microbatches in a simple forward pipeline, total time is approximately (M+P−1)tstage, useful occupancy is M/(M+P−1), and a single request still traverses P stages. For M=1 there is no throughput-filling benefit. Data parallelism instead replicates the whole model: it raises aggregate capacity without accelerating one request. A fleet plan must keep these replica units consistent.

Exercise — When a small collective dominates decode

Use P=8, α=2 μs, m=1 MiB, Blink=200 GB/s, and L=80 with two all-reduces per layer. Estimate the ring time and total collective floor. If sharding saves only 3 ms of local work, does this non-overlapped model predict a latency win?

Show worked solution

Startup is 2·7·2=28 μs. Data time is (14/8)·1,048,576/(200·10⁹)≈9.175 μs. One collective takes approximately 37.175 μs; 160 collectives take 5.948 ms. A 3 ms local saving cannot offset 5.948 ms added communication, so this model predicts a slowdown of about 2.948 ms. Real overlap and collective algorithms may change the result; the calculation exposes the condition that must be measured.

Derivation: derive how many experts a batch actually touches

Uniform routing approximation. There are E experts and each token selects k distinct experts uniformly. Tokens route independently. For a fixed expert, one token misses it with probability 1−k/E; B tokens all miss it with probability (1−k/E)B. Introduce an indicator for each expert being touched and sum expectations:

E[U]=E[1−(1−kE)B]E[ne]=BkEE[Vexpert weights]≈WeE[1−(1−kE)B]Each touched expert is loaded once; E denotes the expert count.\begin{aligned}\mathbb E[U]&=E\left[1-\left(1-\frac kE\right)^B\right]\\\mathbb E[n_e]&=\frac{Bk}E\\\mathbb E[V_{\mathrm{expert\ weights}}]&\approx W_eE\left[1-\left(1-\frac kE\right)^B\right]\\&\text{Each touched expert is loaded once; }E\text{ denotes the expert count.}\end{aligned}E[U]E[ne​]E[Vexpert weights​]​=E[1−(1−Ek​)B]=EBk​≈We​E[1−(1−Ek​)B]Each touched expert is loaded once; E denotes the expert count.​

At small B, a first-order expansion gives approximately Bk touched experts: almost every token causes new expert weights to be loaded, so global batching initially provides limited weight reuse. At large B, the touched count saturates near E while assignments per expert continue to grow. A model’s active parameter count per token therefore does not directly equal the bytes read per batched step. With E=64,k=2,B=32, expected touched experts are 64[1−(31/32)³²]≈40.83, but the mean assignments per expert are only one.

Real routing is neither uniform nor independent. Popular experts can have higher arithmetic intensity but create capacity and load-balance problems; unpopular experts may be loaded for one token. Expert parallelism adds dispatch and combine traffic, so expected expert weight reads are only one part of the cost. Report the token-count histogram and touched-expert count, not just B or the average Bk/E.

5Disaggregation: two phases, two machines

If prefill and decode want opposite things (§0.1), stop making them share.

The architecture: run prefill on one pool of accelerators, decode on another, and ship the KV cache between them over NVLink or RDMA. Each pool gets its own parallelism strategy, its own batch policy, and its own SLO target.

SystemContribution
DistServe (OSDI 2024)Made the case: while colocated, you cannot optimise TTFT and TPOT independently — improving one degrades the other. Co-optimises GPU allocation and parallelism strategy per phase. Their analysis also shows the phases prefer different parallelism (prefill favours intra-op at low arrival rates, inter-op as load rises).
SplitwiseSame split, with layer-level pipelining so KV transfer overlaps computation instead of serialising after it. Also makes the hardware-heterogeneity argument: prefill wants FLOPs, decode wants bandwidth, so they need not be the same SKU.
Mooncake (Kimi)The production version. A KVCache-centric design that pools CPU DRAM, SSD and RDMA into a disaggregated cache, with a global scheduler ("Conductor") that dispatches requests based on where KV blocks already live, replicating or swapping when beneficial. Turns prefix caching into a cluster-wide service.
The cost, which every one of these papers concedes

KV transfer is a first-order cost. A 10,000-token prompt with 327,680 BF16 KV bytes per token carries 3.2768 GB; at a theoretical 400 Gbit/s (50 GB/s) payload rate, transfer alone takes at least 65.536 ms. Layer-by-layer overlap, same-node placement, cache hits, and compression can reduce the uncovered delay. Whether disaggregation pays depends on that delay versus avoided interference and queueing, not on a universal cluster-size threshold.

The hardware implication is the interesting part, and it is now visible commercially: if decode is a bandwidth problem and prefill is a FLOPs problem, they may want different silicon entirely. NVIDIA's non-exclusive licensing agreement with Groq — covering Groq's SRAM-centric LPU technology, alongside hiring its leadership — reads as exactly this bet, with prefill on GPUs and decode routed to bandwidth-optimised parts. (Press reports put the figure at ~$20B; it is a licensing-plus-talent arrangement, not an acquisition, and the number has not been independently confirmed.)

Derivation: derive when transferring KV is worth separating prefill and decode

Uncached prompt transfer. If the prompt has n tokens and c KV bytes per token, total payload is M=nc. A link advertised in bit/s must be divided by eight to obtain byte/s. With effective payload bandwidth Bnet and fixed communication/setup cost t₀, a serial transfer takes at least t₀+M/Bnet. Compression scales M but adds encoding/decoding and metadata.

n=10,000,c=327,680 B/tokenM=nc=3.2768 GBβ=400 Gbit/s=50 GB/s(theoretical one-way)tpayload≥3.276850 s=65.536 msbefore protocol overhead\begin{aligned}n&=10{,}000,\quad c=327{,}680\,\mathrm{B/token}\\M&=nc=3.2768\,\mathrm{GB}\\\beta&=400\,\mathrm{Gbit/s}=50\,\mathrm{GB/s}\quad\text{(theoretical one-way)}\\t_{\mathrm{payload}}&\ge\frac{3.2768}{50}\,\mathrm s=65.536\,\mathrm{ms}\quad\text{before protocol overhead}\end{aligned}nMβtpayload​​=10,000,c=327,680B/token=nc=3.2768GB=400Gbit/s=50GB/s(theoretical one-way)≥503.2768​s=65.536msbefore protocol overhead​

If transfer is pipelined layer by layer, the relevant extra delay can be the uncovered transfer tail rather than the full payload time. In a simplified two-stage stream with total compute time C and transfer time X, perfect overlap approaches max(C,X) plus startup/drain effects, rather than C+X. It cannot beat either total-resource lower bound. Different parallelism layouts may also require KV reshaping or redistribution before decode.

Let disaggregation save Δ milliseconds of interference/queueing at the required SLO, and add uncovered transfer plus scheduling cost Xtail+troute. A latency improvement requires Δ>Xtail+troute under a matched workload. A prefix-cache hit may reduce transferred payload substantially; cache-location-aware routing changes this calculation. There is no universal node-count threshold at which disaggregation becomes worthwhile.

6Speculative decoding: buying tokens with idle FLOPs

The purest expression of the thesis. Decode wastes 99% of the arithmetic units; speculation spends them.

The scheme: a cheap drafter proposes γ\gamma γ tokens; the target model verifies all γ\gamma γ in a single forward pass (they are just a sequence of positions); a rejection-sampling rule accepts the longest correct prefix and guarantees the output distribution is exactly the target model's. It is not an approximation.

Rejection sampling is the classical trick for drawing from a distribution ppp using samples from a different distribution qqq: accept a sample with probability min⁡ ⁣(1,p(x)q(x))\min\!\left(1,\frac{p(x)}{q(x)}\right)min(1,q(x)p(x)​), and on rejection draw from a corrected residual distribution. Applying it token by token is what makes speculative decoding exact rather than an approximation — the reason it is safe to turn on by default. See Appendix B.

E[N]=1−αγ+11−α,α=acceptance rate,γ=draft lengthγ\α0.70.80.942.83.44.183.24.36.1\begin{aligned}\mathbb E[N]&=\frac{1-\alpha^{\gamma+1}}{1-\alpha},\quad\alpha=\text{acceptance rate},\quad\gamma=\text{draft length}\\&\begin{array}{c|ccc}\gamma\backslash\alpha&0.7&0.8&0.9\\4&2.8&3.4&4.1\\8&3.2&4.3&6.1\end{array}\end{aligned}E[N]​=1−α1−αγ+1​,α=acceptance rate,γ=draft lengthγ\α48​0.72.83.2​0.83.44.3​0.94.16.1​​
FamilyHow it draftsTrade-off
Draft modelA small model of the same family (e.g. 1B drafting for 70B)Highest α\alpha α; costs memory and a second model to maintain and align.
MedusaExtra heads on the target model + tree attentionNo second model; α\alpha α lower because the heads predict independently. Reported 2.3–2.8×.

When speculation stops working — and this is the part people miss

Speculation is attractive when extra verified positions cost less than the target invocations they replace. Large short-context batches can be compute saturated and lose throughput, but large long-context batches can remain KV-bandwidth bound and still benefit, as MagicDec demonstrates. Enable and size speculation using measured accepted progress and incremental draft/verification cost for the current batch and context. Batch size alone is not a sufficient criterion.

Derivation: derive expected progress and the marginal speculation decision

Count committed tokens. A round drafts K tokens. Let Ai be the event that the first i proposals survive verification, and let N be emitted tokens including the correction or bonus token. Away from EOS and length caps, N=1+∑i1[Ai]N=1+\sum_i\mathbf1[A_i]N=1+∑i​1[Ai​]. Linearity of expectation does not require independent acceptances:

E[N]=1+∑i=1KPr⁡(Ai)αi=Pr⁡(accept i∣previous accepted),Pr⁡(Ai)=∏j=1iαjαi=α:E[N]={1−αK+11−α,α≠1K+1,α=1\begin{aligned}\mathbb E[N]&=1+\sum_{i=1}^K\Pr(A_i)\\\alpha_i&=\Pr(\text{accept }i\mid\text{previous accepted}),\quad\Pr(A_i)=\prod_{j=1}^i\alpha_j\\\alpha_i=\alpha:\quad\mathbb E[N]&=\begin{cases}\dfrac{1-\alpha^{K+1}}{1-\alpha},&\alpha\ne1\\K+1,&\alpha=1\end{cases}\end{aligned}E[N]αi​αi​=α:E[N]​=1+i=1∑K​Pr(Ai​)=Pr(accept i∣previous accepted),Pr(Ai​)=j=1∏i​αj​=⎩⎨⎧​1−α1−αK+1​,K+1,​α=1α=1​​

Let CK be measured round time, including drafting, verification, cache management, and sampling. Speedup against a serial target step of duration T is TE[N]CK\frac{T\mathbb E[N]}{C_K}CK​TE[N]​, not E[N] alone. Adding one proposal improves the rate only if its survival probability divided by incremental cost exceeds the current rate:

EK+Pr⁡(AK+1)CK+ΔC>EKCK  ⟺  Pr⁡(AK+1)ΔC>EKCK(ΔC>0)\begin{aligned}\frac{E_K+\Pr(A_{K+1})}{C_K+\Delta C}&>\frac{E_K}{C_K}\\\iff\quad\frac{\Pr(A_{K+1})}{\Delta C}&>\frac{E_K}{C_K}\quad(\Delta C>0)\end{aligned}CK​+ΔCEK​+Pr(AK+1​)​⟺ΔCPr(AK+1​)​​>CK​EK​​>CK​EK​​(ΔC>0)​

A larger batch can raise verification cost, but long-context KV-bound decoding can still have useful parallel verification headroom. The decision depends on measured marginal cost, not a blanket batch-size ban. Exact stochastic correctness separately requires the actual proposal law, acceptance min(1,p/q), and positive-residual correction; accepting a high-likelihood draft without that correction is a different contract. See the dedicated speculative-decoding guide for the full coupling proof and tree variants.

Exercise — Should one more draft token be generated?

A K=3 round has conditional acceptance probabilities (0.9,0.8,0.5) and costs 12 ms. An extra proposal would survive conditionally with probability 0.6 and adds 2 ms. Compute both expected emitted lengths and decide whether extending the draft improves tokens/ms.

Show worked solution

Survival probabilities are 0.9,0.9·0.8=0.72, and 0.72·0.5=0.36. Thus E₃=1+0.9+0.72+0.36=2.98 and rate is 2.98/12≈0.24833 tokens/ms. The extra survival probability is 0.36·0.6=0.216, so E₄=3.196 and rate is 3.196/14≈0.22829. Extending hurts: its marginal rate 0.216/2=0.108 is below the existing 0.24833.

7Quantization

The most direct attack on the bandwidth problem: move fewer bytes per parameter.

7.1 What you can quantize, and why each is different

TargetEffectDifficulty
WeightsDirectly reduces the dominant decode byte costEasy. Static distributions, calibrate offline. W4A16 is routine.
ActivationsNeeded to actually use low-precision tensor coresHard. Systematic outliers in a few channels, up to ~100× the typical magnitude.
KV cacheReduces the per-sequence byte cost — raises concurrencyModerate. Keys more sensitive than values; per-channel key scaling helps.
Gradients / optimiserTraining onlyOut of scope here.

7.2 The activation outlier problem

SmoothQuant's insight is worth internalising because it recurs: activations are hard to quantize and weights are easy, so migrate the difficulty. Scale activations down and weights up by a per-channel factor sss, chosen so both become quantizable — an algebraically equivalent, mathematically free transformation that can be folded into the preceding layer's weights.

Y=[Xdiag⁡(s)−1][diag⁡(s)W]=XW,s>0sj=max⁡∣Xj∣αmax⁡∣Wj∣1−α,α≈0.5\begin{aligned}Y&=[X\operatorname{diag}(s)^{-1}][\operatorname{diag}(s)W]=XW,\quad s>0\\s_j&=\frac{\max|X_j|^\alpha}{\max|W_j|^{1-\alpha}},\quad\alpha\approx0.5\end{aligned}Ysj​​=[Xdiag(s)−1][diag(s)W]=XW,s>0=max∣Wj​∣1−αmax∣Xj​∣α​,α≈0.5​

The other major family — GPTQ, AWQ — keeps activations at FP16 and pushes weights to 4 bits, using second-order information or activation-aware channel scaling to decide where precision matters. W4A16 is the standard for memory-constrained single-GPU serving; W8A8 or FP8 for throughput-oriented datacentre serving.

7.3 Formats, and what silicon supports

FormatStructureNotes
FP8 (E4M3/E5M2)Per-tensor or per-block scaleNative from Hopper. The safe default for datacentre inference; accuracy loss is usually negligible with per-block scaling.
NVFP4E2M1 values, 16-element blocks with an FP8 scaleNative on Blackwell. Small blocks track dynamic range tightly, so one outlier contaminates fewer neighbours. 2× FP8 throughput and — more importantly for decode — half the bytes.
MXFP4E2M1 values, 32-element blocks with an E8M0 scaleThe open/portable alternative (OCP standard). Coarser blocks, generally reported slightly behind NVFP4 on accuracy at matched conditions. Choose it when the same artefact must run on multiple vendors.
INT8 / INT4Affine or symmetric with scalesUniversal support, including on older and embedded parts. INT4 weight-only with FP16 activations remains the workhorse for edge.
The hardware lesson from the FP4 generation

Block scaling is central to modern low-bit floating formats. A four-bit E2M1 value has a sign, two exponent bits, and one explicit fraction bit; it does not have a four-bit mantissa. MXFP4 and NVFP4 differ in block size and scale representation, so “shared exponent” does not describe every scale format. Metadata increases effective bits per value and must be included in both storage and traffic. Native low-bit matrix instructions depend on silicon and kernel support; a device without native FP4 arithmetic may still benefit from compressed weight storage followed by dequantization if reduced traffic exceeds conversion cost. It is not guaranteed to have zero speedup.

Derivation: derive why equivalent scaling still changes quantization error

SmoothQuant identity. Let X∈ℝm×d, W∈ℝd×o, and D=diag(s₁,…,sd) with every sj>0. Matrix multiplication is unchanged because D⁻¹D=I: XW=(XD−1)(DW)XW=(XD^{-1})(DW)XW=(XD−1)(DW). Channel j’s activation range scales down by sj, while the corresponding weight-row range scales up by sj.

Set A=XD⁻¹ and B=DW. If quantization introduces errors EA, EB, expand the quantized product and subtract AB:

ΔY=(A+EA)(B+EB)−AB=EAB+AEB+EAEB∥ΔY∥≤∥EA∥∥B∥+∥A∥∥EB∥+∥EA∥∥EB∥For any submultiplicative norm.\begin{aligned}\Delta Y&=(A+E_A)(B+E_B)-AB\\&=E_AB+AE_B+E_AE_B\\\|\Delta Y\|&\le\|E_A\|\|B\|+\|A\|\|E_B\|+\|E_A\|\|E_B\|\\&\text{For any submultiplicative norm.}\end{aligned}ΔY∥ΔY∥​=(A+EA​)(B+EB​)−AB=EA​B+AEB​+EA​EB​≤∥EA​∥∥B∥+∥A∥∥EB​∥+∥EA​∥∥EB​∥For any submultiplicative norm.​

The exact real-arithmetic identity therefore does not imply identical quantized outputs. Changing s moves error between the activation and weight terms. For a uniform unclipped quantizer with step Δ, each scalar rounding error is bounded by Δ/2; clipping, outliers, and group scaling change that bound. The common s formula balances calibrated ranges heuristically; α≈0.5 is not a universal optimum derived from this norm inequality.

Metadata ledger. For N values of b payload bits, groups of g values, and s scale bits per group, storage is Nb+s⌈Ng⌉+metadataNb+s\left\lceil\frac Ng\right\rceil+\mathrm{metadata}Nb+s⌈gN​⌉+metadata bits. Effective bits/value approach b+s/g only when groups are full. NVFP4’s 4-bit values plus an 8-bit scale per 16 values give 4.5 bits/value before outer scales, padding, and layout metadata; MXFP4 with one 8-bit scale per 32 values gives 4.25. Peak low-precision FLOPs, checkpoint bytes, and effective HBM traffic are three separate quantities. A weight-only format can still save bandwidth when arithmetic uses a wider format, provided its dequantization path is efficient.

8.1 What is actually on the floor

PartMemoryBandwidthDense BF16 / FP8 / FP4Ridge (BF16)

H100 SXM and H200 have similar listed peak compute, while their nominal HBM capacity and bandwidth differ. This makes the comparison a useful illustration of the importance of memory resources. A vendor-reported inference speedup is not a controlled proof that memory alone caused the gain: establish the same model, precision, software, tensor parallelism, batch or arrival process, and latency target before attributing the difference quantitatively.

B200 adds a second die (10 TB/s die-to-die), 2.4× H100's bandwidth, and native FP4. Rack-scale (GB200 NVL72: 72 GPUs, ~13.4 TB of pooled memory over NVLink) exists because the unit of deployment for a frontier MoE model is no longer a server.

The B200 capacity above is the current DGX B200 system specification, 1,440 GB across eight GPUs, divided by eight; historical nominal capacity figures may differ. Keep per-GPU and per-system quantities separate. NVIDIA DGX B200 specifications.

Use the ratio of the relevant dense compute peak to effective memory bandwidth for each device and format. A higher compute peak can widen the memory-bound region, while a bandwidth-focused revision can narrow it. The practical question is the workload’s position on that particular roofline, not a rule that every hardware generation changes the balance in one direction.

8.3 Non-GPU approaches, and what each one bets on

ApproachBetConsequence
Google TPULarge systolic arrays, big HBM, tightly coupled optical/torus interconnect; inference-specific generationsExcellent throughput per dollar at scale; less flexible, and you get it through one cloud.
AWS Trainium / InferentiaCost-optimised, huge fleets, tolerable per-chip performanceThe economics play — wins on $/token rather than tokens/s.
Groq LPUAbolish HBM. Hundreds of MB of on-die SRAM as the primary weight store, not a cache; deterministic scheduling, no DRAM controllersExtraordinary decode latency, because SRAM bandwidth is 1–2 orders of magnitude above HBM. But capacity per chip is tiny, so a model must be sharded across many chips, and it is poorly suited to prefill. A pure decode machine.
CerebrasWafer-scale: put the whole model on one piece of silicon with on-wafer SRAMSame bet as Groq at a different granularity — trade capacity and generality for bandwidth.
SambaNovaThree-tier SRAM / HBM / DDR memory hierarchyExplicitly a memory-hierarchy play: keep hot weights close, cold weights cheap.
The pattern across all of them

Every serious non-GPU inference design is a memory architecture decision, not a compute one. Groq and Cerebras replace HBM with SRAM; SambaNova adds a tier; TPU buys more HBM and a better fabric. Nobody's pitch is "more FLOPs." That is the clearest possible confirmation of §0.2 — and it is the reason the industry is now splitting prefill (FLOPs-hungry) from decode (bandwidth-hungry) onto different parts, which is what the NVIDIA–Groq arrangement in §5 institutionalises.

8.4 Designing silicon for inference

If you are specifying an inference part, in rough order of impact:

  1. Bandwidth per FLOP is your headline spec, not FLOPs. Target the ridge point at your intended batch size and precision. A part with a ridge point of 300 FLOP/byte serving a workload at intensity 20 is 93% idle by construction.
  2. Capacity determines concurrency determines cost per token. §1.4 showed a 15× throughput swing from context length alone, purely through how many sequences fit. Every extra GB of HBM is directly monetisable.
  3. Native low precision with block scaling. Not just 4-bit MACs — per-16 or per-32-element scale application in the accumulation path, plus cheap dequantization. The scale handling is the hard part.
  4. A real gather engine. Paged KV, MoE token routing and sparse attention all issue block-granular gathers. A descriptor-driven DMA whose unit is a KV block or an expert tile is worth more than the equivalent area in MACs.
  5. Interconnect sized for all-to-all, not just all-reduce. MoE expert parallelism is the demanding pattern and it is where the frontier is going.
  6. Small-M GEMM efficiency. Decode is B×dB\times dB×d by d×dd\times dd×d with BBB in the tens. A systolic array tuned for 256×256 tiles idles badly. Utilisation at small M is a first-class spec.
  7. Consider specialising. A prefill part and a decode part have almost disjoint requirements. The industry is converging on this; a general-purpose part is a compromise between two workloads that want opposite things.
  8. Don't over-index on dense transformers. Production models are increasingly MoE, hybrid-linear, and sparse-attention. Read the other three guides in this series and ask what each does to your memory system — the answers are different and sometimes contradictory.

At the memory-filled batch, KV traffic is comparable to weight traffic. Cache compression can improve both capacity and bandwidth, but its incremental benefit must be calculated from the current precision, metadata, and latency bottleneck. The fleet size above is an idealized starting bound; a latency-constrained plan uses profiled effective rates and headroom.

Derivation: derive a feasible replica count from both capacity and a latency model

Explicit teaching model. A replica occupies one GPU, holds a full model of W bytes, has C bytes left for KV, and serves equal-length contexts costing k=nc bytes per request. Its step time is approximated by t0+max⁡ ⁣(W+BkBeff,BfFeff)t_0+\max\!\left(\frac{W+Bk}{B_{\mathrm{eff}}},\frac{Bf}{F_{\mathrm{eff}}}\right)t0​+max(Beff​W+Bk​,Feff​Bf​). Effective rates and overhead t₀ must come from profiling. Let the target per-token latency be τ>t₀.

  1. Capacity requires B≤C/k.
  2. The bandwidth term requires W+Bk≤Beff(τ−t₀).
  3. The compute term requires Bf≤Feff(τ−t₀).
  4. Take the integer floor of the minimum positive bound. For U simultaneous active requests, at least ceil(U/B) replicas are needed under the model.
Bmodel=⌊min⁡{Ck,Beff(τ−t0)−Wk,Feff(τ−t0)f}⌋Rmodel≥⌈UBmodel⌉if Bmodel≥1\begin{aligned}B_{\mathrm{model}}&=\left\lfloor\min\left\{\frac Ck,\frac{B_{\mathrm{eff}}(\tau-t_0)-W}k,\frac{F_{\mathrm{eff}}(\tau-t_0)}f\right\}\right\rfloor\\R_{\mathrm{model}}&\ge\left\lceil\frac U{B_{\mathrm{model}}}\right\rceil\quad\text{if }B_{\mathrm{model}}\ge1\end{aligned}Bmodel​Rmodel​​=⌊min{kC​,kBeff​(τ−t0​)−W​,fFeff​(τ−t0​)​}⌋≥⌈Bmodel​U​⌉if Bmodel​≥1​

Using W=70 GB, C=61 GB, k=1.34217728 GB, τ=1/30 s, t₀=3 ms and Beff=0.8·4.8 TB/s, the bandwidth bound is approximately 34.63 requests; the memory bound is approximately 45.45. If the compute bound is looser, choose B=34 and obtain ceil(1000/34)=30 one-GPU replicas. The predicted step is 3 ms+(70+34·1.34217728)/3840 seconds≈33.113 ms. This is a profiled-model planning estimate, not a measured SLO guarantee; arrival bursts, prefill, output growth, and tails require headroom.

A node containing eight such replicas is DP=8. If instead TP=8 is chosen, eight GPUs jointly form one replica: weight/cache sharding, collective time, and per-replica concurrency must all be recomputed. Dividing a one-GPU capacity calculation by eight and then labeling the result TP silently changes the deployment. Likewise, the starting ledger already uses FP8 KV; it cannot receive the same 2× saving again.

Exercise — Find the binding limit and the correct replica unit

A one-GPU replica has C/k=40 memory slots, a bandwidth/SLO limit of 28.7 slots, and a compute/SLO limit of 90 slots. There are 250 simultaneously active requests. How many replicas and eight-GPU nodes are required before headroom? If someone labels these nodes TP=8 without recalculation, what is wrong?

Show worked solution

The binding minimum is 28.7, so the integer batch limit is 28. Replica count is ceil(250/28)=ceil(8.9286)=9. Packing eight independent replicas per node takes ceil(9/8)=2 nodes, with unused slots before any resilience/headroom policy. Calling each node TP=8 would turn eight independent replicas into one distributed replica, invalidating the assumed per-replica memory and timing bounds. TP may be useful, but it needs its own profile and ledger.

10Open problems

  1. Output-length prediction. Scheduling, memory reservation and admission control would all be dramatically better if you knew how long a response will be. Nobody predicts it reliably, and reasoning models with variable-length thinking made it harder.
  2. Serving heterogeneous architectures. Production models increasingly mix dense attention, linear attention, sliding windows and MoE in one stack. Each needs a different kernel, a different cache structure and a different batching policy — in the same request. Serving engines are only beginning to cope.
  3. Composability of optimisations. Paged KV × sparse attention × quantized cache × speculative decoding × chunked prefill is five features that each assume they own the KV layout. Every pair needs bespoke integration; the combinatorics are the real engineering cost of a serving stack.
  4. Agentic and reasoning workloads. Long chains of thought, tool calls, and re-sent growing conversations break every assumption behind current schedulers — which were designed for one prompt in, one answer out. Prefix caching is the current patch, not a design.
  5. Cost models that predict. Simulators exist, but capacity planning is still mostly measurement. A predictive model across batch size, context distribution, parallelism and hardware would be worth a lot.
  6. The bandwidth wall itself. Compute keeps outgrowing bandwidth. Processing-in-memory, 3D-stacked SRAM, photonic interconnect and SRAM-only designs are all bets on the same problem, and none of them has clearly won.

11Reading list

  1. start hereKwon et al. — Efficient Memory Management for LLM Serving with PagedAttention (vLLM) (SOSP 2023). arXiv:2309.06180. §3 is the clearest statement of why serving is memory-bound; the rest is the design that most of the industry now runs.
  2. start hereZhong et al. — DistServe (OSDI 2024). arXiv:2401.09670. §3's phase analysis — including Fig. 3 — is the best quantitative account of the prefill/decode split anywhere.
  3. Agrawal et al. — Sarathi-Serve (OSDI 2024). arXiv:2403.02310. Chunked prefill and stall-free batching; also a good primer on scheduling policies and metrics.
  4. Yu et al. — Orca: A Distributed Serving System for Transformer-Based Generative Models (OSDI 2022). The origin of continuous batching. No arXiv version; find the OSDI paper.
  5. Dao et al. — FlashAttention (arXiv:2205.14135), FlashAttention-2 (arXiv:2307.08691), FlashAttention-3 (arXiv:2407.08608). Read FA-1 for the IO argument, FA-2 for work partitioning, FA-3 for what Hopper-specific asynchrony buys.
  6. Leviathan, Kalman & Matias — Fast Inference from Transformers via Speculative Decoding (ICML 2023). arXiv:2211.17192. §3 gives the acceptance-rate algebra; short and worth doing by hand.
  7. Cai et al. — Medusa (arXiv:2401.10774) and Li et al. — EAGLE (arXiv:2401.15077). Drafting without a draft model; tree attention.
  8. Xiao et al. — SmoothQuant (ICML 2023). arXiv:2211.10438. The activation-outlier problem and the migration trick. Pair with AWQ (arXiv:2306.00978) for the weight-only side.
  9. Qin et al. — Mooncake (arXiv:2407.00079) and Patel et al. — Splitwise (arXiv:2311.18677). Disaggregation as deployed, including the KV-transfer engineering.
  10. Pope et al. — Efficiently Scaling Transformer Inference (MLSys 2023). arXiv:2211.05102. The original analytical treatment of partitioning strategies and their arithmetic — still the best "derive it yourself" paper in the area.
  11. Zheng et al. — SGLang / RadixAttention (arXiv:2312.07104). Prefix caching as a first-class primitive.
  12. Engineering sources worth following: the vLLM blog (the "Anatomy of vLLM" post is an excellent internals tour), the SGLang blog, and NVIDIA's technical posts on NVFP4 and TensorRT-LLM.

A.2 Adding the KV term

The clean result above ignores the KV cache. Reinstating it:
