A.3 Expected tokens under speculative decoding

Assume each drafted token is accepted independently with probability α\alpha α. Draft γ\gamma γ tokens; the number accepted follows a geometric distribution (the number of successes before the first failure, when each trial succeeds independently with probability α\alpha α) capped at γ\gamma γ, and one extra token always comes free from the target model's own distribution at the rejection point.

Pr⁡(accept at least i)=αiE[Naccepted]=∑i=1γαi=α(1−αγ)1−αE[N]=1+E[Naccepted]=1−αγ+11−αc=tdraftttarget,S=E[N]1+γcOptimizing this model favors shorter drafts as c rises, longer as α rises.Typical model-drafter heuristic: γ∈[3,8]; near-free n-gram drafts can be longer.\begin{aligned}\Pr(\text{accept at least }i)&=\alpha^i\\\mathbb E[N_{\mathrm{accepted}}]&=\sum_{i=1}^\gamma\alpha^i=\frac{\alpha(1-\alpha^\gamma)}{1-\alpha}\\\mathbb E[N]&=1+\mathbb E[N_{\mathrm{accepted}}]=\frac{1-\alpha^{\gamma+1}}{1-\alpha}\\c&=\frac{t_{\mathrm{draft}}}{t_{\mathrm{target}}},\quad S=\frac{\mathbb E[N]}{1+\gamma c}\\&\text{Optimizing this model favors shorter drafts as }c\text{ rises, longer as }\alpha\text{ rises.}\\&\text{Typical model-drafter heuristic: }\gamma\in[3,8]\text{; near-free n-gram drafts can be longer.}\end{aligned}Pr(accept at least i)E[Naccepted​]E[N]c​=αi=i=1∑γ​αi=1−αα(1−αγ)​=1+E[Naccepted​]=1−α1−αγ+1​=ttarget​tdraft​​,S=1+γcE[N]​Optimizing this model favors shorter drafts as c rises, longer as α rises.Typical model-drafter heuristic: γ∈[3,8]; near-free n-gram drafts can be longer.​

Note the assumption of independence is optimistic — acceptance is correlated along a draft — so treat these as upper bounds and measure α\alpha α on your own traffic.

A.4 Why MoE decode needs a bigger batch

Beffective,dense=BBeffective,expert≈BkE(balanced routing)BMoE≈BdenseEkfor equal weight arithmetic intensityE=256, k=8:BMoE≈32Bdense\begin{aligned}B_{\mathrm{effective,dense}}&=B\\B_{\mathrm{effective,expert}}&\approx\frac{Bk}E\quad\text{(balanced routing)}\\B_{\mathrm{MoE}}&\approx B_{\mathrm{dense}}\frac Ek\quad\text{for equal weight arithmetic intensity}\\E=256,\ k=8:&\quad B_{\mathrm{MoE}}\approx32B_{\mathrm{dense}}\end{aligned}Beffective,dense​Beffective,expert​BMoE​E=256, k=8:​=B≈EBk​(balanced routing)≈Bdense​kE​for equal weight arithmetic intensityBMoE​≈32Bdense​​

Hence large-scale expert parallelism, aggressive all-to-all optimisation, and why MoE serving is fundamentally a large-deployment technique: a small deployment cannot assemble a batch big enough to make the experts efficient, and pays MoE's memory cost for dense-model arithmetic intensity.

BBackground concepts

The performance-model, GPU, networking and numerics vocabulary this guide assumes. Skip what you know.

B.1 The roofline model, properly

§0.2 uses it as a tool; here is what it actually is. The roofline (Williams, Waterman & Patterson, 2009) is a two-line plot that tells you, for any kernel, whether it is limited by arithmetic or by memory — and therefore which optimisation is worth attempting.

I=FLOPs performedbytes moved(horizontal axis)Fachievable=min⁡(Fpeak,Iβpeak)(vertical axis: FLOP/s)I∗=FpeakβpeakI<I∗:memory-bound; reduce bytes movedI>I∗:compute-bound; reduce arithmeticIncreasing the nonlimiting peak does not improve this ideal roofline bound.\begin{aligned}I&=\frac{\text{FLOPs performed}}{\text{bytes moved}}\quad\text{(horizontal axis)}\\F_{\mathrm{achievable}}&=\min(F_{\mathrm{peak}},I\beta_{\mathrm{peak}})\quad\text{(vertical axis: FLOP/s)}\\I^*&=\frac{F_{\mathrm{peak}}}{\beta_{\mathrm{peak}}}\\I<I^*&:\quad\text{memory-bound; reduce bytes moved}\\I>I^*&:\quad\text{compute-bound; reduce arithmetic}\\&\text{Increasing the nonlimiting peak does not improve this ideal roofline bound.}\end{aligned}IFachievable​I∗I<I∗I>I∗​=bytes movedFLOPs performed​(horizontal axis)=min(Fpeak​,Iβpeak​)(vertical axis: FLOP/s)=βpeak​Fpeak​​:memory-bound; reduce bytes moved:compute-bound; reduce arithmeticIncreasing the nonlimiting peak does not improve this ideal roofline bound.​
  • Why "arithmetic intensity" and not "FLOPs": a kernel doing twice the FLOPs over twice the bytes sits at the same point on the plot and runs at the same efficiency. Only the ratio matters.
  • What "memory-bound" really means: the arithmetic units are idle waiting for data. On an H100 at batch-1 decode they are idle roughly 99.7% of the time. This is not a bug to be fixed with better kernels; it is the position of the workload on the plot.
  • The caveats. The roofline assumes peak bandwidth and peak FLOP/s are simultaneously achievable, ignores latency and occupancy effects, and treats the memory hierarchy as one level. It is a first-order model — right about which resource binds, optimistic about absolute numbers.

B.2 GPU and interconnect vocabulary

TermMeaning, and why it matters here
SM (Streaming Multiprocessor)The independent compute unit — 132 on an H100. If your work has fewer independent items than SMs, most of the chip is idle. This is exactly the problem FlashDecoding solves by splitting the KV dimension. §4.1.
OccupancyHow much of the machine is kept busy. Distinct from being compute-bound: you can be at 100% occupancy and still memory-bound, or have spare FLOPs and no work to fill them.
Warp32 threads executing in lockstep — the real scheduling unit. Divergence within a warp wastes lanes.
GEMM / GEMVGEneral Matrix–Matrix and Matrix–Vector multiply. Prefill is GEMM (big, compute-bound); batch-1 decode is effectively GEMV (each weight used once, memory-bound). Batching turns GEMV back into GEMM — which is the whole point of §1.2.
Tensor coreA unit doing a small fixed-shape matrix multiply–accumulate in one instruction. Fast, but only for supported shapes and precisions; a "skinny" B×dB\times dB×d by d×dd\times dd×d product with BBB in the tens uses a fraction of its capability. This is the "small-M GEMM efficiency" point in §8.4.
CoalescingConsecutive addresses read by a warp merge into one wide transaction. Paged KV breaks this slightly, which is the real cost of PagedAttention. §4.1.
CUDA graphCapturing a whole sequence of kernel launches once and replaying it as one unit. At batch 1, per-kernel launch overhead is a measurable share of a ~15 ms step; graphs remove it. §4.1.
Systolic arrayThe rigid 2-D multiply–accumulate grid used by TPUs and most ASICs — data flows through rhythmically. Superb for dense matmul of the right shape, poor at irregular work. §8.4's warning about small-M utilisation is about exactly this.
HBMHigh Bandwidth Memory: DRAM stacked next to the die. Tens of GB at multiple TB/s. Both its capacity and its bandwidth are the binding constraints in this document.
NVLinkNVIDIA's GPU-to-GPU interconnect: 900 GB/s on Hopper, 1.8 TB/s on Blackwell. Roughly 10–20× a datacentre network link, which is why tensor parallelism stays inside a node. §4.2.
InfiniBand / RDMADatacentre networking, and Remote Direct Memory Access — writing directly into another machine's memory without involving its CPU. How the KV cache moves between prefill and decode pools in a disaggregated deployment. §5.
PCIeThe host bus. PCIe 5 ×16 is ~64 GB/s — about 1/75th of H200 HBM bandwidth. That ratio is why CPU offload works for cold prefix caches and never for live decode. §2.3.
All-reduceA collective where every participant contributes a value and all receive the sum. Two per layer in tensor parallelism, on the critical path — latency-critical and the reason TP needs NVLink.
All-to-allA collective where every participant sends a different message to every other. Required twice per MoE layer to route tokens to their experts and back. The most demanding pattern in the stack and the one that shapes interconnect requirements. §4.2.
Point-to-pointOne sender, one receiver. All pipeline parallelism needs — cheap, and tolerant of slower links.

B.3 Systems, numerics and statistics

TermMeaning
Copy-on-writeAn OS technique: several owners share one physical page until one writes, at which point it gets a private copy. In vLLM this lets many requests share the KV blocks of a common system prompt at zero cost until they diverge. §2.2.
Radix treeA tree keyed by string prefixes, so shared prefixes are stored once and any common prefix can be found quickly. SGLang organises KV blocks this way, making cross-request prefix reuse automatic. §2.2.
Internal / external fragmentationInternal: allocated space inside a block that goes unused (reserving 2048 slots for a 10-token answer). External: free space that exists but is too scattered to satisfy a request. Both are what paging eliminates. §2.1.
SLO, p50/p99Service Level Objective — a latency target you promise to meet. Reported at percentiles: p99 means 99% of requests are faster. Tails matter more than means here, because one stalled decode is visible to a user mid-sentence.
GoodputThroughput counting only requests that met their SLO. A system at 10× throughput that misses every deadline has goodput zero — the reason §0.3 insists a throughput number without a latency constraint is meaningless.
Head-of-line blockingOne long item at the front of a queue delaying everything behind it. A 200K-token prefill blocking short requests is the canonical case, and chunked prefill is the fix. §3.2.
Rejection samplingSampling from ppp using draws from a different qqq: accept with probability min⁡(1,p/q)\min(1,p/q)min(1,p/q), and on rejection draw from a corrected residual. This is what makes speculative decoding produce exactly the target model's distribution rather than an approximation. §6.
Geometric distributionThe number of independent successes before the first failure, when each succeeds with probability α\alpha α. Models how many drafted tokens are accepted, and gives the 1−αγ+11−α\frac{1-\alpha^{\gamma+1}}{1-\alpha}1−α1−αγ+1​ formula. §A.3.
E4M3 / E5M2 / E2M1 / E8M0Floating-point layouts: EEE exponent bits, MMM mantissa bits, plus a sign. E4M3 and E5M2 are the two FP8 variants (more precision vs more range); E2M1 is the 4-bit value format shared by NVFP4 and MXFP4; E8M0 is a pure-exponent 8-bit scale format. §7.3.
Block scalingStoring one shared scale factor per small group of values (16 for NVFP4, 32 for MXFP4) so a few bits of mantissa still cover a wide dynamic range. This — not the 4-bit mantissa — is the actual innovation of the FP4 formats, and it requires scale application in the accumulation path. §7.3.
Per-tensor / per-channel / per-token scalingThe granularity at which quantization scales are computed. Coarser is cheaper to store and apply; finer tolerates outliers better. Activation outliers concentrate in particular channels, which is why per-channel scaling helps and per-tensor does not. §7.2.
OutlierIn this context, activation values in a few channels that are systematically ~100× the typical magnitude. They force a huge quantization range that wastes precision on everything else — the core difficulty in activation quantization, and what SmoothQuant migrates into the weights. §7.2.
Amdahl's lawSpeeding up a part that takes fraction fff of runtime by sss gives overall 1(1−f)+f/s\frac1{(1-f)+f/s}(1−f)+f/s1​. The discipline behind §9: measure the share before optimising the component.

CGlossary

Arithmetic intensityFLOPs per byte moved. Compare against the hardware ridge point to decide whether you are compute- or memory-bound.
BsatB_{\mathrm{sat}}Bsat​Saturation batch size — where decode stops being memory-bound. Fp2 BW\frac{Fp}{2\,\mathrm{BW}}2BWFp​, typically in the hundreds.
Chunked prefillSplitting a long prefill across iterations so it can be co-scheduled with decode without stalling it.
Continuous batchingIteration-level scheduling: retire finished sequences and admit new ones every step, instead of running a fixed batch to completion.
DisaggregationRunning prefill and decode on separate accelerator pools, shipping the KV cache between them.
GoodputRequests per second served within the latency SLO. The only well-posed serving metric.
GQA / MQA / MLAKV-sharing schemes: grouped, single, and low-rank-latent. All exist to shrink the KV cache.
NVFP4 / MXFP44-bit float formats with block-shared scales — 16-element blocks with FP8 scale, and 32-element blocks with E8M0 scale, respectively.
PagedAttentionStoring KV in fixed-size non-contiguous blocks with a per-sequence block table. Virtual memory for the cache.
Prefix cachingReusing the KV of a shared prompt prefix across requests, often organised as a radix tree.
Ridge pointPeak FLOP/s ÷ peak bandwidth. The arithmetic intensity at which a machine transitions from memory- to compute-bound.
TTFT / TPOT / ITLTime to first token; time per output token; inter-token latency (TPOT and ITL are used interchangeably).
Tree attentionVerifying several candidate continuations at once with a modified attention mask, used by Medusa and EAGLE.

DCheck yourself

1. Why is batch-1 decode so inefficient, quantitatively?

Per token it performs ~2N2N2N FLOPs and must read N⋅pN\cdot pN⋅p bytes of weights, so arithmetic intensity is 2/p2/p2/p = 1 FLOP/byte at BF16. An H100's ridge point is ~295 FLOP/byte, so you are using roughly 0.3% of the arithmetic capability. It is not a bad kernel; it is the workload. Every optimisation in this guide raises that ratio, shrinks the bytes, or both. §0.2.

2. When can producing 200 sequence tokens in a batch cost nearly the same time as producing one?

When shared weight traffic dominates, compute remains below its effective ceiling, and batch-dependent KV/activation traffic is small, the weight-read time changes little with batch. Then aggregate throughput grows approximately linearly. The fuller model is t(B)≈max⁡ ⁣[BfF,W+BkBW]t(B)\approx\max\!\left[\frac{Bf}F,\frac{W+Bk}{\mathrm{BW}}\right]t(B)≈max[FBf​,BWW+Bk​]: KV adds a term proportional to B and can prevent a finite saturation batch if fk≤FBW\frac fk\le\frac F{\mathrm{BW}}kf​≤BWF​. Thus 1 versus 200 is an example requiring workload measurements, not a hardware law. §1.2.

3. How can long context reduce aggregate throughput much more than per-user speed, and when does that explanation fail?

At a cache-capacity-limited batch, B is approximately inversely proportional to context n, so total active KV Bn can remain nearly constant. Under that particular comparison, total step traffic and per-user speed may change less than aggregate tokens/s. At fixed B, however, KV-read bytes increase with n, and per-user latency can rise substantially. The weight-read floor is only a lower bound, not a prediction that context never affects latency. Include GQA, precision, attention compute, allocator headroom, and the actual batch policy. §1.4.

4. What does paged KV allocation save, and what waste remains?

It avoids reserving one contiguous maximum-length buffer per request and greatly reduces allocator external fragmentation. A request still has a partially filled final page; page tables, allocation metadata, kernel gathers, and copy-on-write operations have costs. Exact prefix sharing can reduce capacity without automatically removing each query’s attention reads. The right comparison is useful payload divided by allocated bytes under the actual length distribution and block size. §2.

5. Why can a long prefill interrupt streaming, and what determines a useful chunk size?

A scheduler that executes a large prefill in one iteration delays the next decode opportunity for existing requests. Chunking bounds that blocking interval and can combine complementary compute and memory work. The costs do not always overlap perfectly: tensor cores, memory traffic, and scheduling overhead can interfere. Choose a chunk size that fits the measured decode-latency budget after current decode work, then evaluate throughput and tail latency under the arrival process. Sarathi-Serve’s reported gains belong to its benchmark settings. §3.2.

6. When does speculative decoding hurt?

When its draft, verification, correction, cache, and scheduling cost exceeds the value of its accepted progress. The relevant test compares expected emitted tokens per speculative round against its cost relative to ordinary decoding. Compute-saturated workloads can lose throughput, but large batch alone is not a proof of harm: a long-context batch can remain KV-traffic limited and benefit from reuse. Acceptance, context, tree shape, hardware, and active load must be measured together. §6.

7. FP4 halves the bytes and doubles peak FLOPs. Does it make decode more compute-bound?

Weight-only intensity is 2B/p2B/p2B/p, while the ridge is F/BWF/\mathrm{BW}F/BW. If F doubles and p halves, the weight-only saturation batch Fp2 BW\frac{Fp}{2\,\mathrm{BW}}2BWFp​ is unchanged. B200 dense FP4 is about 9 PFLOP/s, so its ridge is about 1,125 FLOP/byte at 8 TB/s. Effective gains depend on KV traffic, metadata, and kernel support. §0.2, §7.3.

8. Why is tensor parallelism often kept on fast intra-node links?

Tensor parallelism puts frequent collectives on the layer critical path, with startup latency and transferred bytes both mattering. Pipeline parallelism instead sends boundary activations between stages and has a different communication/bubble trade. This motivates TP within a fast fabric and PP or DP across slower links, but it is a deployment pattern rather than a requirement. Compare usable one-direction bandwidth, topology, collective algorithms, message sizes, and stage balance; bidirectional marketing totals are not interchangeable with per-link payload bandwidth. §4.2.

9. Which hardware metrics should an inference design compare jointly?

Compare compute F, memory bandwidth BW, capacity, interconnect, and supported precision against the workload. The ridge point is F/BWF/\mathrm{BW}F/BW; bandwidth per FLOP is its inverse. For intensity 20 and ridge 300, the roofline bounds arithmetic utilization near 20/300≈6.7%, without claiming the whole chip is idle. H100/H200 nominal compute and memory specifications illustrate why memory improvements can matter, but vendor throughput differences do not isolate one causal variable without matched software, precision, model, load, and latency constraints. §8.

10. How does expert routing change the batch seen by an MoE weight matrix?

Under balanced routing with E experts and k distinct experts selected per token, the mean assignments per expert are Bk/E. Matching a dense expert-sized matrix’s batch therefore suggests an E/k factor, but this is a mean-field comparison: skew, touched-expert count, grouped GEMMs, shared experts, caching, and communication alter runtime. At small B, only a fraction of experts may be touched; do not assume the full expert pool is always streamed. The useful deployment threshold is empirical, not a theorem that MoE only works at large scale. §4.2, §A.4.
